messages.subject_clean: r/qtl discussion: Inputting a mapping data from another mapping program (JoinMap) in R/qtl
messages.body_plain:
I don't quite understand why you're trying to determine marker order de novo, when you already have a physical map. I would focus on identifying major problems in the physical map, which would generally be large-scale rearrangements rather than the sort of local marker order problems that ripple() can find.

But for 3 and X, there seems to be essentially no recombination and so you won't be able to determine marker order from the genotype data. There are big blocks of un-recombined markers on chr 2 and 4, as well, which I'd clip out before trying to assess the order of the rest. There are a couple of blocks on markers on chr 3 and X with excessive BB genotypes which looks to me like it's maybe a genotyping problem.

Regarding ripple, I presume you're using method="likelihood" which is quite computational intensive as it tries to re-estimate inter-marker distances with every order considered. I'd recommend using the default method="countxo" would should take seconds rather than hours even with window=7.

karl

Hi there,

I was hoping someone could give me some intuition on the effect of including several correlated covariates while searching for qtl i.e. using these covariates simultaneously in scanone(), addqtl().

I know the variance calculations become unstable when using correlated covariates in fitting models (e.g. fitqtl()), but any intuition on how they would affect the search for QTLs using scanone() and the like (e.g. addqtl) would be informative for my purposes.

best,
Saad

messages.body_plain:
Ah. What was confusing to me was that you showed just four columns, but the output of summary(fitqtl), in the "drop one QTL at a time" part, will have seven columns.

The "F value" column is the more traditional statistic for multiple linear regression: the mean regression sum of squares divided by the mean error sum of squares. The mean regression sum of squares is (type III SS) / df, with the values from the first two columns in that row (which you didn't show). The mean error sum of squares is from the "error" row in the "full model result", which is the table that preceded this "drop one qtl at a time" table.

The p-value (F) is derived from that F statistic and the two degrees of freedom. In contrast, Pvalue(Chi2) is derived by taking LOD/(2 log 10) and treating it as approximately chi-squared distributed under the null.

karl

There's no option to include a legend.

> (2) Is it possible to to make the heat map only show colour on the loci that have the LOD above the permutation threshold? I thought it should also be in the setting, right? But o DIDN'T MANAGE.
>

There's a chart option zthresh. Use it like this:

library(qtl)
library(qtlcharts)
data(grav)
grav <- calc.genoprob(grav, step=1)
grav <- reduce2grid(grav)
phecol <- seq(1, nphe(grav), by=5)
times <- attr(grav, "time")[phecol]
out <- scanone(grav, phe=phecol, method="hk")

iplotMScanone(out, times=times, chartOpts=list(zthresh=3))

> (3) I want to add a title to the plot made by 'iplotMScanone'. I tried to add 'caption' in the setting for this command, but it gave me error. Do you know any way to do this?

The caption will give text below the chart.

iplotMScanone(out, times=times, chartOpts=list(zthresh=3,
                                        caption="This is a caption"))

But unfortunately it seems I failed to implement a chart title for iplotMScanone(). Sorry.

karl

messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] "Perhaps it is in basepairs?" warning, but no marker positions given in cross file
messages.body_plain:
R/qtl requires positions, and so if you don’t provide them, it fills them in with a dummy set. If you have a lot of markers, this will lead to the warning about chromosomes being surprisingly long.

It shouldn’t affect the later map construction, and I’ve never seen a problem where linkage maps were smaller than expected.

But if you have a high-quality physical map, I would use that for marker order and not use formLinkageGroups() or orderMarkers(). And if you also have an idea of the chromosomes’ cM length, I would use that to convert Mbp to approximate cM.

I would generally prefer to re-estimate the genetic map (that is, re-estimate the inter-marker distances) before QTL mapping, but it depends on the size of your mapping population and the density of markers. If the markers are very dense, the genetic map doesn’t matter too much. And if the population is rather small, the estimated map won’t be very good.

karl

messages.body_plain:
You could use the function movemarker(), moving the markers one at a time to the position in the female map. Something like this:

female_map <- pull.map(map_athaf2)
for(chr in names(female_map)) {
    pos <- female_map[[chr]]
    markers <- names(pos)
    for(i in seq_along(pos) {
        map_atham2 <- movemarker(map_atham2, markers[i], chr, pos[i])
    }
}

karl

messages.body_plain:
orderMarkers can't be run multicore. You could use the parallel package to have the chromosomes run in parallel, but the approach for a single chromosome can't be parallelized.
